units.title: The digital age: Are we ready?
units.titleZh: 数字时代：我们准备好了吗？

lines.text: You remember a Thursday.
lines.zh: 你想起一个周四。

lines.text: A room by the library courtyard.
lines.zh: 图书馆庭院边的一间教室。

lines.text: Leaf by leaf, the courtyard trees come back.
lines.zh: 庭院里的树，一片叶子一片叶子地回来了。

lines.text: A long table waits, and the chairs are pulled in close.
lines.zh: 一张长桌在等着，椅子都拉得很近。

lines.text: Reach out. Touch what you remember.
lines.zh: 伸手，触碰你记得的东西。

lines.text: Now watch. This is how you were.
lines.zh: 现在，看着吧。当年的你就是这个样子。

lines.text: And then, for the first time, we all laughed together.
lines.zh: 然后，我们第一次一起笑了起来。

epilogue.text: We were so young. And we were learning to listen.
epilogue.zh: 那时我们那么年轻。而我们，正在学着倾听。

sentences: A campus conversation club met each Thursday in a room that looked out over the library courtyard.
Its members could send a message in seconds, yet during shared breaks some sat together without knowing how to begin.
Several said they felt lonely even while their screens filled with names, photos, and alerts.
The club asked a practical question: what kind of connection does this moment need?

notes.line: A campus ____ club met each Thursday in a room that looked out over the library courtyard.

dialog.speaker: lin
dialog.line: So… what do we actually talk about?
dialog.zh: 那……我们到底要聊什么呢？

options.reply: Maybe we start with our purpose. Why are we here?

cues.zh: 一个校园会话社每周四聚会，教室正对着图书馆庭院。
社员们几秒钟就能发出一条消息，可在共同的休息时间里，有些人坐在一起，却不知道怎样开口。
好几个人说，哪怕屏幕上满是名字、照片和提醒，他们还是觉得孤单。
社团提出了一个很实际的问题：这一刻需要怎样的连接？

sentences: To explore it, student organizers designed a four-week listening experiment for learning, not a scientific study.
At each session, members placed their devices in a basket for twenty minutes and took turns describing a small challenge.
The listener had to ask one follow-up question and summarize what they had heard before replying.
The rule felt awkward at first, and some participants were anxious that an urgent message might arrive.

questions.question: What problem led the club to run a listening experiment?
options: The library had banned all electronic devices.
Students wanted to replace every class with a club meeting.
Members felt disconnected despite frequent digital contact.
The group needed to test a new messaging application.
questions.explanation: The club noticed that being constantly connected did not always help people feel heard.

questions.question: What did the listening experiment ask members to do?
options: Stop using every online tool for the whole semester
Put devices away, take turns, and listen before replying
Write a scientific report about phone manufacturers
Replace face-to-face meetings with longer messages
questions.explanation: The club used a short device-free session with turn-taking, a follow-up question, and a summary.

notes.line: The rule felt awkward at first, and some participants were anxious that an urgent ____ might arrive.

notes.zh: 固定的消息查看时段不仅能保护整块阅读时间，也能为紧急联络留出空间。
notes.en: Not only do scheduled message check-in times protect a focused reading block, but they also leave room for urgent contact.

dialog.speaker: rui
dialog.line: Phones in the basket, everyone. For one session, can we stay…
dialog.zh: 手机都放进篮子里吧。就这一次，我们能不能保持……

cues.zh: 为了探索这个问题，学生组织者设计了一项为期四周的倾听实验，目的是学习，而不是科学研究。
每次活动中，成员们把设备放进篮子二十分钟，轮流讲述一个小小的难题。
倾听者必须先追问一个问题，并在回应之前概括自己听到的内容。
这条规则起初让人别扭，有些参与者担心会错过紧急消息。

sentences: By the third session, a pause no longer seemed like a failure; it gave people time to choose words carefully.
Members began noticing tone, hesitation, and the meaning behind a brief answer.
They did not stop using group chats or video calls, which remained useful for planning and maintaining distant friendships.
A quick digital message worked well when information was simple and time was short.

questions.question: What changed by the third listening session?
options: Pauses became useful, and listeners chose their words more carefully.
Participants stopped using online tools for planning.
Every participant agreed that phones should be banned.
The club replaced discussion with written reports.
questions.explanation: The second world describes how participants grew more comfortable with pauses and attentive listening.

notes.line: A quick digital ____ worked well when information was simple and time was short.

notes.zh: 多任务处理似乎节省时间，却可能使我们更难记住谈话的重点。
notes.en: Multitasking may seem to save time, but it can make it harder for us to remember the main point of a conversation.

cues.zh: 到第三次活动时，沉默不再像是一种失败；它给了人们小心斟酌措辞的时间。
成员们开始留意语气、犹豫，以及一句简短回答背后的意思。
他们并没有停用群聊或视频通话，这些工具对于计划安排和维系远方的友谊依然有用。
当信息简单、时间紧迫时，一条快捷的数字消息就很管用。

sentences: A face-to-face conversation offered something different: people could revise an idea, respond to emotion, and build trust.
The club's notes described its own practice, not proof that every student needed the same routine.
That limit made the experiment more useful, because it invited discussion instead of imposing a universal rule.
Readiness for the digital age therefore means choosing a tool with a purpose, rather than treating every notification as a command.

questions.question: What limitation did the organizers place on their notes?
options: They were collected before the activity began.
They measured the quality of the students' devices.
They proved that online friendships were harmful.
They described one club's experience, not a rule for everyone.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly distinguishes local observations from universal scientific proof.

questions.question: According to the final world, what does digital readiness involve?
options: Answering every notification as quickly as possible
Choosing technology according to the purpose of the moment
Avoiding conversation whenever a device is available
Using the same communication routine in every situation
questions.explanation: Readiness is framed as intentional choice: use a tool when it serves the need, and make room for conversation when it matters.

questions.question: What claim did the organizers avoid making?
options: That the club's observations created a universal rule for every student
That conversation can help people build trust
That messages can be useful for simple information
That different situations may call for different tools
questions.explanation: The passage presents the club's notes as local observations, not universal scientific proof.

notes.line: That limit made the ____ more useful, because it invited discussion instead of imposing a universal rule.

notes.zh: 减少不必要的消息提醒有助于学生保护注意力。
notes.en: Reducing unnecessary notifications helps students protect their attention.

cues.zh: 面对面的交谈则提供了不同的东西：人们可以修正想法、回应情绪、建立信任。
社团的记录描述的是它自己的做法，并不证明每个学生都需要同样的日常安排。
这个局限反而让实验更有用，因为它引发的是讨论，而不是强加一条通用的规则。
因此，为数字时代做好准备，意味着带着目的去选择工具，而不是把每一条通知都当作命令。

sentences: On busy days, members used a shared calendar to protect an uninterrupted study session.
On difficult days, they put phones away and asked a friend to listen before giving advice.
Their goal was not less technology, but more intentional communication and a clearer sense of when to converse.
Each Thursday ended with one question: did today's connection help someone feel understood?

questions.question: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: All communication should move to digital platforms.
Devices are harmful and should be removed from campus.
A fast message always creates deeper understanding.
Digital readiness includes choosing a tool that fits the purpose.
questions.explanation: The argument favors intentional choice rather than rejecting technology or responding automatically to every alert.

notes.line: Their goal was not less technology, but more intentional ____ and a clearer sense of when to converse.

notes.zh: 在数字时代，真正的联结不仅取决于网速，还取决于我们是否愿意专注倾听。
notes.en: In the digital age, genuine connection depends not only on internet speed but also on our willingness to communicate and listen attentively.

notes.prompt: Respond to the question: Are we ready for the digital age? State a clear position, support it with one concrete example from student life, and explain how people can balance useful technology with focused attention and meaningful face-to-face interaction.
points: State your position: What does being ready mean beyond owning digital devices?
Develop one student-life example: Show how a notification, platform, or device helps or interrupts learning.
Explain your reasoning: Connect a deliberate habit to attention and face-to-face interaction.
Conclude with one practical principle for responsible digital use.

cues.zh: 忙碌的日子里，成员们用共享日历来保护一段不被打断的学习时间。
艰难的日子里，他们把手机收起来，请朋友先倾听，再给建议。
他们的目标不是减少技术，而是更有意识的沟通，以及更清楚何时该开口交谈。
每个周四都以一个问题收尾：今天的联结，有没有让谁觉得被理解？

lines.text: You remember a room before sunrise.
lines.zh: 你想起一个房间，天还没亮。

lines.text: A small screen is the only light.
lines.zh: 一小块屏幕，是唯一的光。

lines.text: Reach out. Touch what you remember.

lines.text: Now watch. This is how you were.

sentences: For many students, the digital world begins before breakfast, when a notification lights up a device beside the bed.
A student may intend to check one message and then scroll through a platform for several minutes.
An algorithm filters the feed, quietly deciding which stories appear again and which disappear.

questions.question: How can an algorithm shape a student's digital feed?
options: It guarantees that every viewpoint appears equally often.
It decides when a student should sleep.
It removes the need to make privacy choices.
It filters posts and may repeatedly surface selected stories.
questions.explanation: The opening world explains that algorithms filter feeds, so repeated exposure should not be mistaken for a balanced view.

notes.line: For many students, the ____ world begins before breakfast, when a notification lights up a device beside the bed.

notes.zh: 在数字时代，真正的联结不仅取决于网速，还取决于我们是否愿意专注倾听。
notes.en: In the digital age, genuine connection depends not only on internet speed but also on our willingness to communicate and listen attentively.

sentences: Because the stream feels personal, users can mistake repeated exposure for a balanced view of the world.
That is why digital literacy starts with attention: notice what a platform asks you to do, and decide whether it deserves the next minute.
A first-year class tested a simple habit plan for two weeks, keeping short notes on when they checked screens during study.
They found that opening a device between tasks often made it harder to return to the original question.
Trying to multitask did not remove the work; it scattered the attention needed to understand complex ideas.

questions.question: Why did students schedule set times to check messages?
options: To avoid communicating with classmates altogether
To make it easier to return attention to the study task
To make every virtual meeting longer
To remove all notifications from their devices
questions.explanation: The class found that opening a device between tasks made it harder to resume the original question.

notes.line: They found that opening a ____ between tasks often made it harder to return to the original question.

notes.zh: 多任务处理似乎节省时间，却可能使我们更难记住谈话的重点。
notes.en: Multitasking may seem to save time, but it can make it harder for us to remember the main point of a conversation.

sentences: The students began grouping messages into set check-in times and placing one offline study block on their daily schedule.
One student found virtual study groups useful, provided that members agreed on a goal before joining.
Another reviewed privacy settings after learning how much information a default profile could reveal.
A cyber safety instructor asked the class to treat each link, password request, and public post as a choice with consequences.

questions.question: What did the cyber safety instructor ask students to consider?
options: Whether a link, request, or post has consequences before they act
Whether all public posts should be deleted
How to avoid using a platform for school work
Why a privacy setting makes every online choice safe
questions.explanation: The instructor teaches deliberate choices about links, password requests, and public posts.

notes.line: The students began grouping ____ into set check-in times and placing one offline study block on their daily schedule.

sentences: The lesson was not to fear every platform but to understand how its tools filter information and shape habits.
When a data leak or unwanted contact occurs, prevention is valuable; afterwards, calm reporting and account changes matter too.
Students also discussed screen addiction without using the term as a casual label for every long evening online.
A habit becomes concerning when it repeatedly harms sleep, learning, or relationships and a person cannot easily adjust it.

notes.line: Students also discussed screen ____ without using the term as a casual label for every long evening online.

notes.zh: 固定的消息查看时段不仅能保护整块阅读时间，也能为紧急联络留出空间。
notes.en: Not only do scheduled message check-in times protect a focused reading block, but they also leave room for urgent contact.

sentences: Restored balance came from small changes: a mindful walk between lectures, a device-free meal, and a clear end time for study.
During an offline hour, roommates noticed more interaction and solved small disagreements before they grew.
These routines did not make the internet less powerful; they helped students use it more deliberately.
Living well online is not a contest to stay disconnected, but a practice of protecting attention, privacy, and human presence.

questions.question: Which practice helped students restore balance?
options: Checking each message as soon as it arrives
Joining several virtual groups at once
Keeping a device-free meal and a clear end time for study
Treating every long evening online as an addiction
questions.explanation: Small planned routines, including offline time, helped protect attention, rest, and interaction.

notes.line: Restored balance came from small changes: a ____ walk between lectures, a device-free meal, and a clear end time for study.

notes.zh: 减少不必要的消息提醒有助于学生保护注意力。
notes.en: Reducing unnecessary notifications helps students protect their attention.

lines.text: You remember a small clinic in the mountains.
lines.zh: 你想起山里的那间小诊室。

lines.text: On the screen, a doctor is already waiting.
lines.zh: 屏幕那头，医生已经在等了。

lines.text: Reach out. Touch what you remember.
lines.zh: 伸手，触碰你记得的东西。

lines.text: Now watch. This is how you were.
lines.zh: 现在，看着吧。当年的你就是这个样子。

sentences: This original practice story is set in a fictional mountain county, where the nearest specialist clinic is several hours from some villages.
A local health center wanted older residents to receive advice without turning every checkup into a long journey.
It partnered with doctors in a coastal teaching hospital and used a secure telemedicine platform to review basic scans.
The small team added a familiar phone and a private room so patients could ask questions with a nurse nearby.

questions.question: What was the local health center trying to make easier?
options: Replacing all local staff with a remote application
Moving older residents to the coastal city
Making routine specialist advice available without an unnecessary long trip
Collecting health information for public social media
questions.explanation: The first world introduces a local service designed to reduce avoidable travel for routine advice.

notes.line: It partnered with doctors in a coastal teaching hospital and used a secure telemedicine ____ to review basic scans.

notes.zh: 固定的消息查看时段不仅能保护整块阅读时间，也能为紧急联络留出空间。
notes.en: Not only do scheduled message check-in times protect a focused reading block, but they also leave room for urgent contact.

sentences: At first, the technology was only one part of a bigger plan.
Local staff helped residents learn how to place the device, describe symptoms, and ask for a second explanation.
When a connection failed, the center recorded questions and arranged a call-back instead of pretending the screen had solved everything.
Doctors reviewed images carefully and sent written guidance to local clinicians, who remained responsible for follow-up care.

questions.question: Who remained responsible for follow-up care?
options: The local clinicians
The patient's distant family members alone
The makers of the telemedicine device
An automated platform without a medical team
questions.explanation: Remote doctors reviewed information, while local clinicians stayed responsible for follow-up.

notes.line: Doctors reviewed images ____ and sent written guidance to local clinicians, who remained responsible for follow-up care.

notes.zh: 减少不必要的消息提醒有助于学生保护注意力。
notes.en: Reducing unnecessary notifications helps students protect their attention.

sentences: A daughter living far away could join one appointment, but the patient still chose what information to share.
The process respected privacy as well as distance.
This fictional example does not claim that every village has the same service or that online advice can replace an examination.
It shows why human communication matters when a new tool enters healthcare.

questions.question: What limitation does the passage acknowledge about telemedicine?
options: It works only when every patient owns the same phone.
It removes the need to protect private information.
It makes local health professionals unnecessary.
It cannot replace every examination or suit every village.
questions.explanation: The third world warns that online advice is not a universal substitute for in-person examination.

notes.line: The process respected ____ as well as distance.

sentences: The clinic kept an offline option for people who lacked a suitable phone, steady signal, or confidence using an app.
Volunteers explained how the service worked, while medical staff checked whether the advice was clear and useful.
Gradually, families spent less time arranging travel for routine questions and more time planning care with local professionals.
The change depended on trust, accessible design, and patient choice rather than on a device alone.

notes.line: The change depended on trust, accessible design, and patient choice rather than on a ____ alone.

notes.zh: 多任务处理似乎节省时间，却可能使我们更难记住谈话的重点。
notes.en: Multitasking may seem to save time, but it can make it harder for us to remember the main point of a conversation.

sentences: Stories of China can include this kind of practical innovation: people using knowledge and technology to solve a local need.
Its value is measured not by how advanced a screen looks, but by whether residents can participate safely.
A shared project becomes stronger when city doctors, county clinicians, families, and public services each take a clear role.
In that sense, digital progress is a human achievement: it expands connection while keeping dignity, responsibility, and community in view.

questions.question: How does the final world define meaningful digital progress?
options: By the number of screens installed in a community
By whether residents can participate safely and with dignity
By how quickly a remote platform can process every request
By replacing community services with one central system
questions.explanation: The conclusion measures progress by safe, dignified participation and shared responsibility, not by devices alone.

notes.line: In that sense, ____ progress is a human achievement: it expands connection while keeping dignity, responsibility, and community in view.

notes.zh: 在数字时代，真正的联结不仅取决于网速，还取决于我们是否愿意专注倾听。
notes.en: In the digital age, genuine connection depends not only on internet speed but also on our willingness to communicate and listen attentively.

lines.text: You remember an exhibit called Lives in Motion.
lines.zh: 你想起一个叫“流动的人生”的展览。

lines.text: Two lives, one lesson.
lines.zh: 两种人生，一个转折。

lines.text: Reach out. Touch what you remember.
lines.zh: 伸手，触碰你记得的东西。

lines.text: Now watch. This is how you were.
lines.zh: 现在，看着吧。当年的你就是这个样子。

sentences: The class opened an exhibit called Lives in Motion in the campus archive, where biographies were read as sequences of choices.
Its task was not to rank remarkable people, but to ask which evidence could explain a turning point.
One case followed Zheng He, the explorer whose fleet traveled across Indian Ocean routes in the early fifteenth century.
Another introduced Audrey Hepburn, whose public portrait later became linked to a humanitarian mission for children.

questions.question: Why did the students organize the exhibit around choices and evidence?
options: To rank famous people by the size of their audience.
To replace historical sources with dramatic portraits.
To examine evidence that explains the subjects' choices and turning points.
To prove that every biography follows one pattern.
questions.explanation: The exhibit asks readers to connect choices with evidence instead of ranking people or inventing a universal model.

questions.question: Why did students arrange the exhibit around choices instead of ranking the subjects?
options: To show that one person's career is always superior.
To identify evidence that helps explain important turning points.
To avoid discussing the sources behind each biography.
To prove that every life follows the same sequence.
questions.explanation: The exhibit focuses on choices and the evidence that can explain them, not on ranking people.

notes.line: Another introduced Audrey Hepburn, whose public portrait later became linked to a humanitarian ____ for children.

notes.zh: 那位率领船队的探险家留下了值得后人研究的遗产。
notes.en: The explorer who led the fleet left a legacy worth studying.

sentences: Though the lives belonged to different eras and different professions, students searched for a shared question: what does service require?
The first group placed maps and port names beside a short narrative of the voyage.
Records show that trade goods moved across sea routes, yet a map cannot tell every story of the people along them.

questions.question: Which materials helped the class follow the explorer's voyage?
options: Maps, port names, and records of exchanged goods
A movie script and an imagined speech
A portrait with no dates or source note
A list of modern travel advertisements
questions.explanation: The passage names maps, ports, and trade records as evidence for tracing the route.

questions.question: What did the map help students do, and what could it not do?
options: It proved every motive and recorded every conversation.
It replaced written accounts and all historical research.
It showed that every port had an identical purpose.
It helped trace routes but could not tell every person's experience.
questions.explanation: The passage uses maps to trace routes while noting that they cannot capture every story or motive.

notes.line: The first group placed maps and port names beside a short ____ of the voyage.

notes.zh: 一幅优雅的肖像无法讲述一个人的全部人生。
notes.en: An elegant portrait cannot tell the whole story of a person's life.

sentences: Students marked documented details in blue and their own interpretations in amber.
This color code helped them witness the difference between a source and a conclusion.
It also kept the display from presenting one simple motive as the whole explanation.
In the second case, the class examined why an ambitious performer might use fame to draw attention to children's needs.
They learned that Hepburn served UNICEF as Goodwill Ambassador and traveled to Ethiopia in 1988 to highlight the drought's effects.

questions.question: What did the class learn from Hepburn's public mission?
options: One visitor can solve every part of a humanitarian crisis.
A public portrait is enough to explain a whole life.
Fame removes the need to check historical evidence.
Public attention can support a cause but is not a complete solution.
questions.explanation: The mission drew attention to children's needs while the class avoided claiming that one person could end a crisis.

questions.question: What did the 1988 Ethiopia example help the class understand?
options: A public mission can draw attention without solving a crisis by itself.
A famous visitor can replace all local organizations.
A portrait provides enough evidence to explain a humanitarian issue.
Public figures should never speak about children's needs.
questions.explanation: The students distinguish drawing attention from claiming that one person can solve a complex crisis.

notes.line: This color code helped them ____ the difference between a source and a conclusion.

sentences: Her work did not mean one visitor could solve a complex crisis.
It showed how compassion and sustained attention could support a wider humanitarian effort.
Students compared what the sources stated with what a reader might only infer.
When they turned to the final wall, neither figure seemed like a ready-made model for every life.

notes.line: It showed how compassion and sustained attention could support a wider ____ effort.

notes.zh: 学生打开展览时，已经比较了两篇人物传记。
notes.en: By the time the students opened the exhibit, they had compared two biographies.

sentences: The students could admire particular choices without treating a famous person as perfect.
They described a legacy as influence people inherit, question, and sometimes continue in new ways.
The exhibit's narrative joined evidence, context, and consequences instead of relying on a dramatic portrait.
Each visitor left with one question about ambition, responsibility, and the next action they could take.

questions.question: How does the exhibit define a meaningful legacy?
options: As a perfect legend that readers should never question.
As influence that people can inherit, examine, and continue.
As public recognition without evidence or context.
As a single career path everyone should follow.
questions.explanation: The ending treats legacy as an influence that invites evidence-based reflection and responsible action.

questions.question: Which idea best summarizes the exhibit?
options: Famous people should be copied without questioning their choices.
A legacy is only a record of public attention.
Read biographies through evidence, context, and consequences.
Different eras make comparison impossible.
questions.explanation: The final sentences present biography as evidence-based interpretation that can inform responsible choices.

notes.line: The students could ____ particular choices without treating a famous person as perfect.

notes.zh: 有证据支持的叙述能启发读者，也能提醒他们区分事实与推断。
notes.en: A narrative supported by evidence can inspire readers and remind them to distinguish facts from inferences.

points: Introduce the two people and the context

Compare a choice, obstacle, or act of service

sections.title: Audrey Hepburn — a real angel in the world

lines.text: You remember a small gallery, and a familiar face.

lines.text: You remember a bookstore in the old harbor district.
lines.zh: 你想起老港区的一家书店。

lines.text: Lantern Books. Twenty years, and then a recession.
lines.zh: 灯笼书店。二十年，然后是一场衰退。

sentences: In the old harbor district, Lantern Books had served students for twenty years, but a recession changed the street.
Inflation pushed up rent and delivery costs, while a tight budget left fewer new titles on its shelves.
Owner Mei wrote each expense beside the supply of books and the demand from readers instead of guessing.
Her savings covered only two months, and she feared the shop would close before the next school term.

questions.question: Which pressures first put Lantern Books at risk?
options: A sudden surplus of books and lower delivery costs
A plan to move the store to a larger building
Rising rent and delivery costs during a recession, alongside a tight budget
A new rule requiring every reader to buy a book
questions.explanation: The opening links the recession and inflation to higher rent and delivery costs, while the budget and savings are shrinking.

questions.question: Why did the team borrow a second drill instead of buying one immediately?
options: The community center refused to lend any equipment.
Residents were not allowed to repair anything themselves.
The log showed that immediate demand did not yet justify a permanent purchase.
The cooperative wanted to remove all maintenance records.
questions.explanation: The group checked real use and planned repairs, then borrowed a second drill for a short-term need instead of assuming a purchase was necessary.

notes.line: Owner Mei wrote each expense beside the supply of books and the ____ from readers instead of guessing.

notes.zh: 规则越清晰，资源就越容易公平地流动。
notes.en: The clearer the rules are, the more fairly resources circulate.

sentences: To understand the crisis, she asked customers what they needed and what they could afford.
A campus club suggested a sharing wall where a reader could leave one book and choose another.
Mei took a small loan to build weatherproof shelves and a simple checkout desk.
During a two-week pilot, every exchange was entered in a paper ledger with a fair, affordable fee.

questions.question: What did Mei and the campus club build to respond to readers' needs?
options: A larger shop stocked only brand-new titles.
A book-sharing wall, funded by a small loan and run as a measured pilot.
A delivery service that charged readers before showing the books.
A private club that stopped serving neighborhood consumers.
questions.explanation: Mei used a small loan to build weatherproof shelves, then the club tracked exchanges during a two-week pilot.

Reusing books improved efficiency, but cleaning, sorting, and missing-copy checks still required staff time.

questions.question: Why did the exchange not automatically mean higher profit or effortless service?
options: Cleaning, sorting, and checking missing copies still took staff time.
No readers wanted to reuse books after the first day.
The shop stopped keeping any records of its inventory.
The club required every customer to buy two new titles.

questions.question: What did the drill's use after a repair-workshop announcement show?

Residents prefer to buy a new tool every time.
The lending room no longer needed maintenance.
Demand always stays the same regardless of timing or information.

notes.line: Rather than call the project an instant success, Mei compared its modest ____ with saved purchasing costs.

sentences: Some consumers could not pay even a small fee, so the club created a no-fee exchange hour.
The change widened access without hiding the real cost of keeping the service open.
Mei explained that sharing works only when rules protect both the resource and the people using it.
By the end of the term, the shop had not become rich, yet it had kept two local jobs and reopened a quiet reading corner.

questions.question: Which change addressed the access problem for residents who worked late?
options: The team bought more tools for storage.
The membership fee was doubled.

Students traced how price, supply, demand, and access shaped ordinary choices in the neighborhood.
They left with a practical lesson: a healthy economy depends on choices that keep value circulating and responsibility visible.

questions.question: What best explains the bookstore's modest resilience by the end of term?
options: A single investment guaranteed a large profit.
The neighborhood no longer needed affordable reading.
The shop stopped listening to customers and club members.
Trust, clear records, cooperation, and repeated adjustments kept value circulating.
questions.explanation: The ending credits resilience to trust, records, repair, and adjustment, not a guaranteed windfall.

questions.question: What is the passage's main conclusion about sharing?
options: Shared resources require no rules or upkeep.
Sharing works better when access, responsibility, records, and feedback are balanced.
A fee automatically guarantees a fair outcome.
Every frequently used object should be purchased at once.
questions.explanation: The final sentences define sharing as choices about access, responsibility, and value, supported by clear rules and feedback.

notes.line: They left with a practical lesson: a healthy ____ depends on choices that keep value circulating and responsibility visible.

sentences: On campus, a club found that students often bought a required book for one term and then let it collect dust.
They designed a sharing exchange where members could lend or swap a copy through a staffed locker.

questions.question: What was the campus club's first goal for its book exchange?
options: To promise instant revenue to every member
To replace the campus library with a commercial store
To make useful books affordable and keep them circulating among readers
To collect damaged books without recording their condition

notes.line: ____ shifted around exam weeks, so the club added high-use titles and asked departments to donate older editions.

Members compared user feedback, wait times, damaged copies, and costs before changing the rules.

Page Loop taught them that sharing works best when transparency makes responsibility as visible as convenience.

Compare access, maintenance costs, local-shop support, and user feedback over time.

lines.text: You remember a county library on a quiet afternoon.
lines.zh: 你想起一个安静的下午，一所县城图书馆。

lines.text: The fan turned slowly. Someone was reading by the window.
lines.zh: 旧风扇慢慢转着，有人靠窗读书。

lines.text: Reach out. Touch what you remember.
lines.zh: 伸手，触碰你记得的东西。

lines.zh: 现在，看着吧。当年的你就是这个样子。

sentences: For a class project, students created a fictional county case called Yunhe to examine access to reading during a downturn.
In their story, many families had a tight budget, and the county library could not buy every new title.
The students proposed a shared digital-lending catalog so one licensed copy could reach more readers over time.
They did not present Yunhe as a documented real event; it was a model for testing choices, costs, and access.
Their first question was simple: who might still be left out if the service moved online?

questions.question: In the students' fictional county case, what first made reading harder for families?
options: A sudden increase in free transport to the library
Lower household budgets and the cost of buying every title separately

A lack of interest in reading among all age groups

questions.question: Why did the library keep an assisted, offline option alongside digital lending?

Offline service always costs less than maintaining a digital catalog.

notes.line: The team listed the ____: licenses, devices, staff time, network access, and community knowledge.

notes.zh: 规则越清晰，资源就越容易公平地流动。
notes.en: The clearer the rules are, the more fairly resources circulate.

sentences: A local school offered quiet study space, and a community group helped troubleshoot basic device problems.
These partners could not erase the recession, but they reduced barriers that price alone could not explain.
The library also collected feedback in short interviews, including from people who had not used the service.
Their comments led to clearer instructions, larger text, and a weekly in-person help session.
One student argued that digital lending was always more efficient, but the access notes challenged that claim.

questions.question: How did cooperation improve the service rather than merely add publicity?

The library transferred all decisions to one sponsor.
Residents stopped reporting problems with access.
Readers, volunteers, and librarians found barriers and adjusted the service together.

Sustained reading access, manageable costs, and useful feedback from different residents
